Acquisition / Customer experience

Before you increase the budget, inspect the journey.

A framework for deciding whether the next investment belongs in reach, relevance or the next action.

By Sreshta Joshi

When a campaign is underperforming, increasing the budget is one of the easiest decisions to make. It is also a decision that deserves a better diagnosis.

The useful question is where the next investment would change the outcome. That could be reach, a more relevant message, a clearer page or a better follow-up. Those are different problems, even when the headline symptom is the same.

Start with the outcome being counted.

A click, an enquiry, an enrolment and a qualified opportunity are different signals. Before using campaign performance to make an investment decision, define what the platform counts and what the business needs.

At REMIC, my acquisition work included rebuilding Search and Performance Max with value-based bidding and tighter query controls. The recorded results were 45,800 clicks and 2,260 tracked conversions at $35 CPA, with a 21% CTR improvement. Those figures describe campaign activity and economics. Understanding their business meaning also requires the conversion definition and the reporting period.

This distinction is useful because a platform can report a healthy number while the commercial team is looking at something else. The task is to connect the two views clearly enough to decide what to do.

Inspect three points in the journey.

1. Who is arriving?

Review search intent, targeting and the questions people bring to the campaign. Are they looking for the product, exploring the category or seeking something the business cannot provide? More reach can amplify a targeting problem.

2. What are they being promised?

Read the ad, the page and the offer together. A strong message should make the relevance easy to understand. If each part introduces a different proposition, the person has to do unnecessary work to connect them.

3. What happens next?

Follow the journey after the first response. Examine the form, purchase step, email or sales handoff. A campaign might attract relevant people while the next step introduces friction. In that situation, improving the journey could be a more useful next investment than buying additional visits.

Choose a test that answers the diagnosis.

Once the likely problem is clear, set a bounded test. Name the audience, the change, the owner and the review window. Decide what would count as support for the hypothesis before the test begins.

If the hypothesis concerns intent, test query controls or targeting. If it concerns clarity, review the message and page. If it concerns follow-up, examine the handoff. Running several unrelated changes together makes it harder to understand which decision affected the outcome.

Keep the limits visible.

Campaign performance can change with seasonality, demand, the offer and the available data. A short test may suggest a direction without establishing a durable result. A useful review should name those limits and look for supporting evidence from the customer journey and the commercial team.

Budget can help a working system reach more people. The decision becomes stronger when the system has been examined first.
